pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the volunteer program in this workspace. Share it with the volunteer coordinator, each program lead and anyone who runs a shift.
: every applicant and volunteer, their area, the days they can come, skills, background check and waiver, emergency contact and total hours.
: every shift with its place, people needed, minimum age, spots left and hours given.
: who signed up for which shift, whether they came, and their hours.
: the onboarding steps each new volunteer still needs.
: company teams, school clubs and faith groups who come together.
New applicants are called within three days and their training steps added.
On Monday the coordinator fills the week's short shifts.
Shift leads take attendance and hours at the end of every shift.
On Friday the coordinator reviews the Dashboard: short shifts, checks to chase, hours given.
Every morning: shifts today and sign-ups to confirm
Every Monday: shifts with spots left this week and next
Every month: background checks requested or expired, volunteers on break
Every quarter: hours and value of volunteer time for funders and the board

The coordinator owns recruiting, screening and the schedule. Program leads own their shifts and their volunteers' training. Shift leads take attendance. The program manager reads the hours report for grants.

Phone numbers, emails and emergency contacts are confidential. Keep only the status and the date of a background check here, never the report itself. Share the workspace with staff and leads, not with every volunteer.
Rename areas, skills and training steps to match your program and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place and drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
The program at a glance. Charts read the live tables.

Training rows for that volunteer not marked done
No one works alone with open safeguarding or safety training

text.text: Most volunteers who quit do so in their first month, usually because nobody called them back or their first shift was confusing. A quick, warm onboarding fixes both.
The person fills in the volunteer form. Call or email within three days; a week of silence loses half of them.
and add their training steps: orientation for everyone, a safety walk-through for the tool library and market, the safeguarding module and a background check for anyone working with children.
Once every training step is Done or Waived, press
. Book their first shift with an experienced volunteer beside them.
Anyone who will be alone with children, handle money on their own, or drive for the alliance needs a cleared check before their first shift. Set
to Requested when you send the form and to Cleared when the result comes back, then write the

date (most programs renew every two or three years). The Dashboard lists every check that is requested or expired. Never put the check results themselves in this workspace; keep only the status and the date.
Every volunteer signs the liability waiver before their first shift. Tick
. Volunteers under 18 need a parent or guardian to sign as well.
Fitting the person to the work
Ask about the days they are free and what they are good at, then fill in
. A retired carpenter belongs at the repair evening; a Spanish speaker is gold at the market info table. People stay when the work fits them.
Name tag ready and the shift lead told who is coming
Where to park, what to wear, who to ask for
A real task for the first hour, not standing around
A thank-you text the same evening

Marguerite applies to read with children. The coordinator calls her the next day, books orientation for Thursday, sends the background check form and the safeguarding module, and pencils her into story hour beside Lupe. Two weeks later her check is cleared, every training step is done, and she is active.
A good shift starts before anyone arrives. The lead knows who is coming, the work is ready, and every hour is written down at the end.

includes that day and whose skills fit.
Send a reminder to everyone signed up, with the place, the start time and what to bring.
for the shift; parents bringing children need to know ahead.
Sign-in sheet or tablet at the door
Name tags and a five-minute welcome, with the safety points for the task
New volunteers paired with someone experienced
Water, gloves and a place for bags
Keep everyone busy; idle volunteers do not come back.
Take a photo of the work, with permission, for the newsletter.
Thank people by name before they leave.
Anyone who did not show: a friendly message, not a scolding. Two no-shows in a row and the coordinator checks in.
Funders and city grants ask for volunteer hours and their value. Each volunteer's
multiplies hours by a national value of a volunteer hour; change the rate in the formula to your state's figure. Hours recorded the same day are accurate; hours guessed a month later are not.

Saturday market setup needs six people and has four. On Thursday the coordinator messages three weekend regulars who list lifting as a skill; two say yes. On Saturday the lead marks five attended and one no-show, enters three hours each, and the market report for the city grant fills itself in.
Volunteers do not stay for the pizza. They stay because the work matters, someone noticed what they did, and they made friends. Plan all three.
A text after a first shift: what they did and why it helped.
A handwritten card at 25, 50 and 100 hours. Sort Volunteers by hours given to see who is close.
A short story in the newsletter each month about one volunteer, with their permission.
column reads each person's attended shifts against no-shows. "Check in" means it is time for a friendly call: schedules change, and the fix is often a different day or area. Volunteers on
get a note every three months with no pressure to return.
Long-time volunteers want responsibility. Ask your steadiest people to lead a shift, train newcomers, or run a group volunteer day. Leading is the strongest reason people stay for years.

Company teams and school clubs bring many hands at once. Treat the group contact like a donor: confirm the project two weeks out, send the waiver link, have work ready for every person, and send photos and the hours afterward. Many companies match their employees' hours with a grant; ask.
An appreciation evening during national volunteer week in April
A one-page report to every volunteer: hours given, what changed because of them
A short survey: what to keep, what to change, what they wish they could do
When someone retires, thank them in person and mark them
rather than deleting them. Their history stays, and many return.

Theo reaches 100 hours at the tool library. The lead mentions it at the Thursday desk, the coordinator sends a card, and Theo is asked to run the next repair evening. He says yes and brings a friend who signs up the same night.
